newsitem.title: BULGARIA: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT TAKES OVER, INHERITS CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT TAKES OVER, INHERITS CRISIS.

text.p: Bulgaria's outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev formally handed over to his successor Petar Stoyanov at a modest ceremony in Sofia on Wednesday.

Stoyanov took over command of the army from Zhelev, the first directly-elected head of state in Bulgaria's 1,300-year history, at a military parade outside the presidency, attended by political leaders and foreign diplomats.
The 44-year-old lawyer inherits severe economic crisis and political deadlock that has prevented formation of a new government.
He cancelled the usual champagne reception as inappropriate at a time when hundreds of thousands of Bulgarians are hungry.
The army sends conscripts home at weekends so their families can feed them.
The opposition has held 15 days of street protests for quick elections and against formation of a new cabinet by the ex-communist Socialists, who have a majority in parliament.
Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in presidential polls last November, backed opposition calls for quick elections at his swearing-in ceremony in parliament on Sunday.

He has already begun mediation efforts and both government and opposition hope the new president, whose legal speciality is divorce, can break the deadlock over formation of a new cabinet and the date for a general election.
"I hope the new president will be more efficient in resolving our problems," said housewife Roumyana Petrova, one of a small crowd watching the ceremony, which was broadcast on national television.
Zhelev, a dissident philosopher and one of the key figures in Bulgaria's transition from one-party rule, lost a U.S.-style primary to Stoyanov last June.
"The new president looks more impressive than the previous one and I hope that his actions will be as statesmanlike as he looks," said engineer Petar Ivanov.
Later on Wednesday Stoyanov will lay a wreath at the tomb of the unknown warrior to commemorate Bulgaria's war dead and swear an oath on the Gospel at one of Sofia's medieval churches.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but want to form a second cabinet following the resignation of prime minister Zhan Videnov on December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.
Videnov on Tuesday urged Stoyanov to hand the mandate to the Socialists' nominee for premier, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, saying he had a programme ready to bring the country out of crisis.
The opposition blames Videnov for leading the country to the verge of default on its $10 billion foreign debt.

Government corruption and resistance to reform have left Bulgaria lagging behind other eastern European states. Annual inflation is running at more than 300 percent and a flight into dollars has pushed the lev to a new all-time low on Wednesday of 800 to the dollar from about 70 a year ago.
In his final address to the nation as president, Zhelev laid the blame on the country's ex-communist rulers, and on the constitution, which places most power in the hands of parliament.
"Bulgaria's model of transition failed because for seven years economic and social reforms were not carried out. Instead of coming out of the crisis, Bulgaria is sinking lower," he said.
Zhelev, who last year founded a new political party, said he would work in his retirement for the expansion of the president's powers.
